explanations.answer: The emperor Claudius ordered all Jews out
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Aquila and Priscilla had just come from Italy because Claudius, the Roman emperor, had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Nobody packs for a move like that on a whim. I once got moved out of a kitchen drawer, so I know a little about being sent somewhere you didn't plan.

explanations.answer: A great famine struck the whole city
explanations.explanation: I get why a famine sounds believable, since empty cupboards make people move. But the text names no famine. It says Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2). That was an order, and it came from the emperor himself.

explanations.answer: A fire burned their whole street down
explanations.explanation: A fire would be a rough way to lose a home, friend. But the text mentions no fire at all. It says that Claudius, the emperor, had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome (Acts 18:2). That order is why Aquila and Priscilla showed up in Corinth.

explanations.answer: They're tentmakers by trade like him
explanations.explanation: Right on the money, baker. The text says Aquila and Priscilla were tentmakers by trade, just as Paul was. Same trade, so staying and working with them made sense. When I find somebody else who loves a good rolling pin, I'm there all day too.

explanations.answer: They're old friends from his hometown
explanations.explanation: That would be a sweet reunion, friend. But the text says Paul found them there in Corinth, and it never calls them old friends from home. What it gives is the reason: they were tentmakers by trade, just as he was. Sometimes a shared trade is all it takes to start a good partnership.

explanations.answer: They're relatives on his mother's side
explanations.explanation: I like the family angle, baker, but the text never says they were related. It says Paul found a Jew named Aquila and went to visit him and his wife Priscilla. He stayed and worked with them because they were tentmakers by trade, just as he was.

Close, friend, but the text says more than that. Every Sabbath Paul reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade Jews and Greeks alike. So the Greeks were in that room too. The room had a bigger crowd than you'd think.
Yes, baker. The text says Paul was trying to persuade Jews and Greeks alike, every Sabbath. So the synagogue crowd wasn't only Jews. Paul was talking to both groups.
That's the one, baker. Paul was testifying to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. Once Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, he devoted himself fully to the word.

I see where that came from, friend, but it's not what the text says. Paul testified to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ (Acts 18:5). That happened after Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia. The Christ is the title he put in front of them.

Good guess, but there's no angel in this verse, baker. After Silas and Timothy came down from Macedonia, Paul devoted himself fully to the word. He testified to the Jews that Jesus is the Christ. It's one short line, and it's the center of the verse.
You've got it, baker. Paul told them, “From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. The insults at the synagogue were the moment he said it.

I can see why you'd pick them, friend, but the Samaritans don't show up in this passage. Paul said, “From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” Gentiles are people who aren't Jews. He said it right after he was opposed and insulted.

The Pharisees aren't named anywhere in this passage, baker. Paul said, “From now on I will go to the Gentiles.” That means people who aren't Jews, and he said it after the opposition and insults. He shook out his garments first, which is about as clear as a message gets.

explanations.answer: The house of Titus Justus next door
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God. He didn't have far to walk. I think that was a pretty short commute for such a big change.

explanations.answer: The house of Jason in Thessalonica
explanations.explanation: Jason does show up earlier in Paul's travels, in Thessalonica (Acts 17:5). But this scene is in Corinth. Paul left the synagogue and went next door to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God. No long trip needed, friend.
That's a long way back, baker. Paul had already left Athens and gone to Corinth (Acts 18:1). After leaving the synagogue, he only went next door, to the house of Titus Justus, a worshiper of God.

True, baker. Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his whole household believed in the Lord. The man in charge of the synagogue, and his whole household with him! Paul had left that synagogue after being opposed and insulted (Acts 18:6), and still its leader believed. I'd have needed to sit down.

Not this time, friend. The text says Crispus, the synagogue leader, and his whole household believed in the Lord. That's the same synagogue Paul had just walked out of. So the leader's own household believed.

Yes, baker. Many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized. Hearing, believing, baptism: the verse lays it out in that order. That's a lot of people packed into one sentence.

I know Paul's stories have plenty of arrests, friend, but not in this verse. The text says many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized. It's a happy line, so we can enjoy it. The trouble comes later in the passage.

Scattered? Nobody gets scattered in this verse, baker. The text says many of the Corinthians who heard the message believed and were baptized (Acts 18:8). I think it's the happiest line in the whole passage, so I'm not letting anyone scatter it.

That's right, baker. The Lord told Paul in a vision, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent.” Three short commands, back to back. I think a man who'd just been opposed and insulted could use all three.

Pride isn't what the Lord brings up here, friend. He told Paul in a vision, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent.” The word is afraid. After the opposition Paul had faced, that was the word the Lord chose.
Anger isn't in the vision, baker. The Lord told Paul, “Do not be afraid; keep on speaking; do not be silent.” So the word is afraid. He spoke it to Paul one night, in a vision.

explanations.answer: He has many people in this city
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The Lord said, “For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many people in this city.” Two promises in one line: He is with Paul, and no one will lay a hand on him. The reason He gives is that He has many people in this city.

The text gives no word about guards, friend. The Lord's reason is this: “For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many people in this city.” The promise rests on the Lord's own words, not on anybody's respect.

That's a nice thought, baker, but the Lord doesn't say it. He told Paul, “For I am with you and no one will lay a hand on you, because I have many people in this city.” The reason He gives for no one laying a hand on Paul is that He has many people in this city.

You got it, baker. Paul stayed for a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians. That's a long stretch in one place. I've spent longer than that stuck in the back of a junk drawer, so I know a long stay.
That's too short, friend. The text says Paul stayed for a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians. Three months is a small slice of that. He settled in for the long haul.

That's too long for this stop, baker. The text says Paul stayed for a year and a half, teaching the word of God among the Corinthians (Acts 18:11). Still a good long stay, though. It's half the time you picked.

The Areopagus is back in Athens, friend (Acts 17:19). This scene is in Corinth. The Jews brought Paul before the judgment seat while Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, a Roman official over the region.

The synagogue is where Paul reasoned on the Sabbath, baker, but that's not where this goes. The Jews coordinated an attack on Paul and brought him before the judgment seat. That's a place for a ruling, and Gallio, the proconsul of Achaia, was there.
It might seem that way, baker, but the text doesn't show it. Just as Paul was about to speak, Gallio, the proconsul, told the Jews his answer. The text gives no defense from Paul in that scene.

That's right, baker. Just as Paul was about to speak, Gallio, the proconsul, spoke to the Jews instead. The text gives no defense from Paul in that scene. I think that was a strange moment, being ready to talk and then not needed.

explanations.answer: A dispute about words and their own law
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. Gallio told the Jews, “But since it is a dispute about words and names and your own law, settle it yourselves.” He's saying it isn't a wrongdoing or vicious crime. To him, it was a matter for them to sort out.

explanations.answer: A quarrel over who owns the synagogue
explanations.explanation: Nobody's fighting over the synagogue keys here, friend. Gallio calls it “…a dispute about words and names and your own law…” (Acts 18:15). I think the keys were safe the whole time. He just wants no part of it, and he sends them off to settle it themselves.

explanations.answer: A fight between two families over land
explanations.explanation: Land? Nobody's fighting about land, baker. Gallio calls it “…a dispute about words and names and your own law…” (Acts 18:15). I bet he'd have been just as done with a land fight. He says he refuses to be a judge of such things.
True, baker. Gallio said, “…settle it yourselves.” Then he added, “I refuse to be a judge of such things.” He was the proconsul sitting at the judgment seat, and he still handed it back.
That's not how it goes, friend. Gallio told the Jews, “…settle it yourselves. I refuse to be a judge of such things.” So he handed the matter right back to them. He wanted no part of it.

I understand wanting that, baker, because this part is heavy. But the text says the crowd seized Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beat him in front of the judgment seat. Then it says, “But none of this was of concern to Gallio.” He did not step in.

That's right, baker. This part is heavy. The crowd seized Sosthenes, the synagogue leader, and beat him in front of the judgment seat. The text says, “But none of this was of concern to Gallio.” I think it's a hard thing to read, and Paul's story isn't over yet.
